newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Avmin seeks more Zambia copper assets - paper.
newsitem.headline: Avmin seeks more Zambia copper assets - paper.

text.p: Avmin Ltd is leading an international consortium that is bidding for the bulk of working assets in the privatisation of Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM), Business Day said on Friday.

The minerals division of South African mining house Anglovaal Ltd, which has already won the right to develop the Konkola North copper reserve, is now looking at acquiring working assets including ZCCM's Nchanga and Nkana divisions.
Avmin's partners in the bid for these assets include Phelps Dodge Corp and Noranda Inc, the report said.

Nchanga and Nkana produced 225,000 tonnes of copper in the last financial year, roughly half of ZCCM's total output. The divisions include several open pit and underground copper mines, a copper tailings treatment plant, a concentrator and a cobalt treatment plant and smelter.
An Avmin spokesman declined to comment "at this stage".

Business Day said that if the bid succeeded Avmin could have, via direct and indirect control, about 33 percent of ZCCM's assets. This includes the right to develop the Konkola North deposit, which is estimated to be worth $500 million.
One analyst said: "it would be a coup for Avmin to secure this deal. The Nkana and Nchanga divisions are the jewel in the crown of ZCCM."
Earlier this month a consortium led by Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd said it was prepared to buy a majority shareholding in Zambia's Konkola Deep copper mine.

Mining analysts believe the Zambian mining industry could be set for a renaissance following privatisation with production set to surge over the next 15 years to more than a million tonnes of copper a year from around 400,000 at present.

Development of the two Konkola mines is seen as crucial to the rehabilitation of the mining industry -- once one of the biggest producers of copper and cobalt in the world but now only the seventh-biggest producer of copper.
The Zambian government hopes the privatisation of ZCCM -- which accounts for about 90 percent of Zambia's foreign earnings -- will turn around the country's economy.
